title: Walk the house before you hire anyone
summary: A slow walk with a notepad shows what to fix, what to tell buyers, and what to leave alone.
body: Start at the street. Look at the roof edge, the walkway, and the front door. Write down what you see before you explain it away.
Inside, run every faucet, flip every light, and open every window that should open. Note stains, soft floors, and doors that stick. One line per issue.

Sort the list into three piles: safety and function, things that will show up in photos, and projects you will not do. Ask for written bids on the jobs you cannot price yourself. A bid is a number you can type into the proceeds calculator. A hunch is not.
steps: Walk once with the lights on and once in daylight.
Write one line per issue.
Mark each line: fix, disclose, or leave.

title: Fix function before you spend on finish
summary: Repair leaks, heat, and latches before you buy paint.
body: Leaks, heat, cooling, loose steps, and dead outlets come before paint. A fresh coat on a damp wall does not hold, and buyers notice a door that will not latch.
If a system is near the end of its life, get it in writing and decide whether you will repair it or describe it in your disclosure. Do not hide it behind a rug.
Small function fixes are the ones people test on a first visit: a drain that clears, a garage door that reverses, a handrail that does not wobble.
steps: Stop active leaks first.
Test smoke and carbon-monoxide alarms.
Plan paint and floors only after the function list is done.

title: Clear surfaces before you add anything
summary: Empty counters and floors do more for a showing than extra decor.
body: Buyers are trying to see the room. Pack until each room has one job: sleeping, cooking, eating, or sitting.
Leave a few useful pieces. A made bed, a table that fits, and a lamp that works are enough. Take extra chairs out if the path is tight.
Store packed boxes outside the photo frame. A dining room full of bins reads as a storage room.
steps: Clear counters down to one or two useful items.
Pull furniture off the main walking path.
Keep packed boxes out of the rooms you will photograph.

title: Pack personal items before the first showing
summary: Box photos, mail, and papers so the rooms show the house.
body: Personal photos, mail, and collections pull attention away from the property. Box them before the first photographer or visitor arrives.
Take names, notes, and calendars off the refrigerator. Close closets you do not want opened, and do not overstuff the ones you leave.
Leave a simple path from the front door through the main rooms. If you still live there, pick one cupboard for daily items and keep the rest clear on showing days.
steps: Box personal papers and photos.
Clear the refrigerator door.
Walk from the front door to the back of the house and move anything that blocks the path.

title: Price the property you have
summary: Compare sold homes that match this property, then write the net you will accept.
body: Pull recent sold listings that match this house on facts you can check: bedroom count, bathrooms, size, lot, garage, age, and the updates the listing described.
Active listings are asking prices. Sold listings are closed prices. Use the closed ones as your comparison set, then adjust for condition you can see in the photos and at the property.

Write three numbers before you pick a list price: the price you will advertise, the net you hope to clear, and the lowest net you will accept. The lowest net belongs in the proceeds calculator, using your payoff and your costs.
steps: Compare at least three sold properties with similar facts.
Adjust for condition you can point to, not for a story.
Write the bottom net before the first offer.

title: Leave room to answer a real offer
summary: Set the list price with room for a credit and still hit your net.
body: A list price is the number on the ad. Your net is the decision. Price, credits, and timing move together.
If you set the list price at the exact dollar you need to walk away with, the first repair credit puts you under your line.
Decide in advance which givebacks you can live with: a repair credit, a closing-cost credit, or a later closing date. Write them down while you are calm.
steps: Keep the list price and the net you need on two separate lines.
Pick two terms you can flex on and one you will not.
Recalculate proceeds every time a credit changes.

title: Take listing photos in daylight with the lights on
summary: Open the shades, turn on the lamps, and keep the camera level.
body: The camera needs light. Open the window coverings and turn on the overhead lights and the lamps you are leaving.
Shoot when you can see the corners of the room. Glare on bare glass can wash a wall out. Wait for the sun to move off that window, or shoot that room from a different corner.
Stand in a corner and keep the camera level. If the walls lean in the frame, the room looks smaller than it is. Close toilet lids, move trash cans, and coil the hose if it sits in the front photo.
steps: Clean the windows you will shoot through.
Turn on the lights before you frame the shot.
Take one wide photo and one detail photo in each main room.

title: Photograph the work you finished
summary: Give finished repairs their own clear photo, and lead with the front of the house.
body: People scroll quickly. A clear photo of a repaired step, a new faucet, or the label on a replaced water heater answers a question before the showing.
Do not feature a project you have not finished. An open wall belongs in the disclosure conversation, not as the first image.
Lead the set with the best daylight photo of the front. Then show the kitchen, each bathroom, and the main living space before the extra rooms.
steps: Put the front of the house first.
Include one clear photo of each bathroom and the kitchen.
Retake any shot where the repair is blurry or dark.

title: List the jobs before you pick who does them
summary: Write every job in a sale, then decide who will do it and what it costs you.
body: Hiring an agent and selling it yourself are two ways to cover the same work: pricing, photos, showings, disclosure forms, offer review, negotiation, and closing coordination.

Next to each job, write the name of the person who will do it and what it will cost you in hours or dollars. Use your own rates in the commission comparison. This site does not fill in a rate for you.
If you sell it yourself, you can still offer to pay a buyer’s agent. That choice is a line you enter. It is not a requirement and it is not a default.
steps: Make two columns: the job, and who owns it.
Ask any agent you interview for a written list of what they will do.
Decide who owns each job before you order a sign.

title: Questions to answer if you sell it yourself
summary: Forms, showings, and offer review are still yours if you sell without an agent.
body: Find out which disclosure forms your state expects. A local attorney or the closing company can tell you which forms apply. This site cannot.
Decide how a buyer books a showing, where you will be during the visit, and what you will put away first. Set hours you can actually keep.
Plan the offer path before the first one arrives: who receives the contract, who reads it with you, and how quickly you will answer.
steps: Ask a closing company what they need from a seller who has no agent.
Write your showing hours down.
Have an attorney or agent review the first contract before you sign it.

title: Read the whole offer before you answer the price
summary: Credits, dates, and contingencies change the money more than the headline price.
body: Find the purchase price, seller credits, earnest money, financing terms, and every date. Read those before you react to the price alone.
A higher price with a large credit can leave you with less than a lower price with no credit. Run both sets of numbers through the proceeds calculator before you reply.
A repair request is a request. It is not a promise you already made. List what you will do, what you will credit, and what you will decline.
steps: Highlight every dollar that leaves your side.
Highlight every deadline.
Ask your agent or attorney what each contingency lets the buyer do.

title: Compare net and dates before you counter
summary: Put each offer on one row and counter the gap in your net.
body: Make one row per offer: price, credits, closing date, and what has to happen first, such as an inspection, an appraisal, or a loan approval.
Choose the row that meets the net you wrote down and a timeline you can move on. If none do, counter the specific gap in plain numbers.
Answer before the offer expires. If you need more time, ask for it in writing. Do not let a deadline pass in silence if you still want that offer.
steps: Build one comparison row per offer.
Recalculate proceeds after every counter.
Send your answer in writing.

title: Build the closing folder before you have a buyer
summary: Collect payoff contacts, receipts, and a wire-check plan before you are under contract.
body: Start a folder, paper or digital, for the mortgage servicer’s payoff phone number, the association contact if you have one, warranty paperwork you plan to transfer, and receipts for repairs you are disclosing.
Keep your disclosure draft in that folder and update it when a repair is finished. The version you sign should match the house on signing day.
Ask the closing company how they send wire instructions. Plan to confirm those instructions by calling a phone number you look up yourself, not a number that arrived only in an email.
steps: Give the folder one home and label each document.
Request the payoff when you have a contract and a closing date.
Call the closing office to confirm wiring instructions before you send money.

title: Walk the house again before the buyer’s final visit
summary: Check the fixtures you promised to leave, and report anything that broke.
body: Test the lights, the appliances you are leaving, and the faucets. Replace bulbs that are out. The final walkthrough is easier when you have already done this.
Remove trash, leftover paint, and hardware you are not including. The contract says what stays. Do not remove a fixture you agreed to leave.
If something broke after you signed, tell the buyer in writing before they find it. A surprise at the walkthrough is harder to solve than a note sent the day before.
steps: Use the same room list you used for showings.
Leave remotes, keys, and codes where the contract says they go.
Do a last pass for personal papers in drawers.

title: Book the move after the closing date is real
summary: Wait for a contract date, then book the truck with a written backup plan.
body: A target date can move. Put a deposit on a mover when the closing date is in the contract, and ask what happens if that date shifts by a day or two. Get the answer in writing.
Measure sofas, mattresses, and tables that might not fit through the next door. Do this before the truck is in the driveway.

If you are packing yourself, start with rooms you do not use every day. Keep a first-night box in your car: chargers, a change of clothes, basic tools, and anything you need before the truck is unpacked.
steps: Confirm the closing date with the closing company before you book.
Get the mover’s cancellation terms in writing.
Pack the first-night box and keep it with you.

title: Label boxes by the room they go to
summary: Name the room on two sides of every box and keep a first-night box with you.
body: Write the room and a short contents line. “Kitchen — pans” is enough. Write it on two sides so a stack does not hide the label.
Number the boxes and keep a simple list on your phone or on paper. When a box is missing, the number tells you what to ask about.
Carry documents, jewelry, and spare keys in the car. Do not put them on the truck.
steps: Label at least two sides of each box.
Number the boxes and keep the list.
Load the first-night box last so it comes off first.

title: Replace cracked caulk before photo day
summary: Cracked caulk shows up in close photos. Replace it while the repair list is still short.
body: Look along tubs, showers, and the kitchen sink. Cracked or missing caulk reads as a leak even when the wall behind it is dry.
Remove the old bead, let the joint dry, and lay a new one. A thin, smooth line photographs better than a thick smear.
If you find soft drywall while you are there, stop and treat that as a leak repair, not a caulk job. Put it on the function list.
steps: Check every wet joint with the lights on.
Recaulk only after the joint is dry.
Photograph the finished joint for your repair folder.

title: Finish the entry before the rest of the house
summary: The front door and entry are the first rooms a visitor stands in. Finish those before the back closets.
body: Wash the door, polish or replace tired hardware, and make sure the house numbers can be read from the street. A stuck storm door is a first impression you can fix in an afternoon.
Clear shoes, mail, and coats down to what you use this week. One mat and a working light are enough.
If you only have one day before photos, spend it on the entry, the kitchen counters, and the main bathroom. Leave the deep closet for later.
steps: Clean the door and the hardware.
Check that the entry light works.
Remove the daily clutter before every showing, not only before the photo shoot.

title: Write your bottom line before the first showing
summary: Write the lowest net you will accept, and do it before anyone asks.
body: Open the proceeds calculator and type your payoff, the commissions you expect to pay, closing costs, credits, and repairs. The result is a draft of your net, not a promise.
Write the lowest net you will accept on paper and put it with your offer checklist. Change it only when a real number in the deal changes.
When an offer arrives, you already know which gaps matter. You will not have to invent a bottom line while someone waits on the phone.
steps: Enter your own costs in the calculator.
Write the lowest acceptable net where you can find it.
Update it when the payoff or a credit changes, not when you feel rushed.

title: Keep the camera level and skip the distortion
summary: A tilted wide shot makes a straight room look small. Keep the camera level.
body: Hold the phone or camera at about chest height and level with the floor. If you tilt up, the ceiling takes over the photo. If you tilt down, the floor does.
Step back before you zoom with your feet. Extreme wide angles bow straight lines. A buyer who visits will notice that the room does not match the picture.
Take two frames of each room and keep the one where the door casing is vertical. Delete the other so it does not end up in the listing by mistake.
steps: Use a level line in the room, such as a door frame, to check the camera.
Shoot from a corner, not from the middle of the room.
Keep the frame that matches what a person sees when they walk in.

title: Put every deadline on one page
summary: Every offer has dates. Put them on one page so none expire in silence.
body: Copy each date out of the contract onto one page: offer expiration, earnest-money due date, inspection end, appraisal, loan commitment, and closing.
Add the name of the person who has to act. A date with no owner is easy to miss.
Check the page every morning while you are under contract. If a date is close and you are not ready, call your agent, attorney, or the closing company that day.
steps: Transfer dates the hour you receive an offer or a counter.
Name an owner for each date.
Look at the page before you agree to a new credit or a new closing day.

title: Call the closing office before you wire
summary: Look up the closing office and call them before you send a wire.
body: Wire instructions that arrive by email can be altered. Treat a last-minute change of bank details as a stop sign.

Look up the closing company’s phone number on its own site or on the paperwork you received at the start, then call. Read the routing number and account number back. Do not use a phone number that was only in the email.
If anything does not match, do not send the wire. Ask the closing officer to reissue the instructions in the way they normally do.
steps: Save the closing company’s main phone number when you open the file.
Call that number and read the wire details back.
Refuse rushed changes that you cannot confirm on the phone.

title: Deep-clean after the dusty work, not before
summary: Clean after the dusty repairs, not before. Archived because the prep tips now cover the order of work.
body: Sanding, patching, and caulk throw dust. If you deep-clean first, you will clean again after the last repair.
Do the messy jobs, let the dust settle, then clean top to bottom: lights and trim, then counters, then floors. Save the floor for last so you are not tracking grit back across it.
This note stays in the archive so the order is still written down. The active prep tips now carry the same sequence: function first, finish next, clean before photos.
steps: Finish dusty repairs before the deep clean.
Clean from the top of the room toward the floor.
Schedule photos after the floors are dry.

title: Test the alarms before you list
summary: Press each smoke and carbon-monoxide alarm, and replace any battery that fails.
body: Walk every floor and press the test button on each alarm. Write down the room if one stays quiet or chirps.
Replace the battery, then test again. If it still fails, replace the alarm and note the date on your repair list.
Keep the receipt with your other repair papers. A working alarm is a function item, not a decorating project.
steps: Press every alarm and write down the quiet ones.
Replace the battery or the alarm, then test again.
File the receipt with your repair papers.

title: Clear the gutters before showings
summary: Empty the gutters and check that downspouts send water away from the foundation.
body: Look along the roof edge after a dry day. Leaves and grit in a gutter spill over the siding in the next rain.
Scoop the debris, then run a hose at the high end. Water should travel to the downspout and land several feet from the wall.
If water pools at the foundation, add an extension. Write the fix on your repair list before you spend on paint.
steps: Scoop leaves and grit from the gutters.
Run a hose and watch where the water lands.
Add a downspout extension if water sits by the wall.

title: Tighten loose hardware before the first visit
summary: Snug the hinges, handles, and cabinet pulls that rattle when someone opens a door.
body: Open every door and drawer once. A loose hinge or a wobbly pull is a small job that shows up in a walk-through.
Tighten the screws you can reach. If a screw spins in the hole, move it slightly or use a longer screw so it bites.
Skip new hardware unless a piece is broken. Function comes before a matching set.
steps: Open every door and drawer.
Tighten screws that move.
Replace only pieces that are broken.

title: Trace a stain to its source
summary: Find the leak that made the stain, then repair that before you paint over the mark.
body: A ceiling spot or a bubbled patch of paint usually means water was there. Painting the mark hides it for a week.
Check the fixture, the roof above, and the supply line. If you cannot find the source, hire someone who can and get the cause in writing.
After the source is dry and repaired, then patch and paint. Keep the invoice so you can tell a buyer what was fixed.
steps: Mark each stain on your walk-through list.
Repair the leak before you paint.
Save the invoice with your other receipts.

title: Run the heat and the cooling before showings
summary: Turn each system on, listen for a short cycle, and change a dirty filter.
body: Set the heat and let it run until the air at a vent is warm. Then switch to cooling if the house has it, and wait for cool air.
A filter clogged with dust makes the system short-cycle. Slide in a clean filter and write the size on the filter frame for next time.
If a system will not start, put that on the repair list before photo day. A quiet system is easier to explain than a dead one.
steps: Run heat until a vent is warm.
Run cooling until a vent is cool, if you have it.
Replace a dirty filter and note any system that will not start.

title: Leave a clear path through each room
summary: Move chairs and baskets so a visitor can walk in, turn around, and see the floor.
body: Stand in each doorway. If you have to step sideways to enter, the room reads as smaller than it is.
Slide extra chairs, hampers, and floor baskets out for showings. You can put them back when the day is over.
Leave one comfortable seat if the room is a living room. The goal is a path, not an empty box.
steps: Stand in each doorway and look for a straight path.
Move pieces that block the walk.
Keep one seat where people actually sit.

title: Open the window coverings the same way
summary: Raise every shade to the same height so the light looks even from room to room.
body: Walk the house and set each shade, blind, or curtain the same way. One closed room next to a bright one looks accidental.
If a covering is broken, take it down for showings rather than leaving it crooked. A bare window is easier to read than a stuck blind.
Do this before photos and again the morning of a showing. It takes a few minutes and it is one of the first things people notice.
steps: Set every covering to the same height.
Remove a covering that will not hang straight.
Check them again the morning of a showing.

title: Put pet gear away before showings
summary: Move bowls, beds, and litter out of sight, and air the rooms they sat in.
body: Pet gear tells a visitor about your routine, not about the room. Box the bowls, beds, and toys before the first appointment.
Wash the floor where bowls sat. Open a window for a few minutes if a litter area has a smell.
If the pet will be home, plan a quiet room or a sitter for showing hours so doors can stay open.
steps: Box bowls, beds, and toys.
Clean the floor where they sat.
Plan where the pet will be during showings.

title: Stop after one simple table setting
summary: A plain setting on the table is enough. Extra decor on every surface works against you.
body: If you set the dining table, use plates you already own and leave the center clear. Then stop.
Do not add pillows, throws, and new art in the same week you are clearing clutter. The rooms should look lived-in and open.
Take a photo of the table from the doorway. If the setting is the first thing you see, remove it.
steps: Use dishes you already own.
Leave the center of the table clear.
Remove the setting if it dominates the photo.

title: Leave closets partly empty
summary: Take out enough clothes and boxes that a visitor can see the rod and the floor.
body: A closet packed to the ceiling hides the storage you are selling. Move out-of-season clothes to boxes you will take with you.
Leave a gap on the rod and a clear patch of floor. Do the same for a linen shelf: fold a few stacks, not a wall of towels.
You do not need to show an empty closet. Half full reads as usable.
steps: Box what you will not wear during showings.
Leave a gap on the rod and a clear patch of floor.
Fold linen into a few stacks.

title: Write three numbers before you list
summary: Write the list price, the net you hope for, and the net that would make you walk away.
body: Use the proceeds calculator with numbers you choose. Run it once at the price you might list, and once at a lower price.
Write both nets on one page, plus the net where you would rather stay put. Those three numbers are yours.
Do this before you talk with an agent or a buyer. A conversation is easier when the page already exists.
steps: Run the calculator at two prices you might list.
Write the net you hope for and the net where you would stop.
Keep that page with your offer notes.

title: List credits before you pick a price
summary: Write the repairs and concessions you already expect, then see what they do to your net.
body: A list price that ignores a likely credit is a guess. Write the items a buyer might ask you to pay: a repair you already know about, a closing cost you are willing to cover, or a credit for something you will not fix.
Type those amounts into the calculator as seller credits or repairs. The net that remains is closer to a decision.
You can change the list later. You cannot change it wisely if the credits were never written down.
steps: Write the credits you already expect.
Enter them in the calculator.
Read the net before you choose a list price.

title: Match what was included in a sold home
summary: Before you compare a sold price, write what that sale included and what yours includes.
body: Two houses can sell for different amounts because one included appliances, a credit, or a repair. The headline price does not say which.
For each sold home you are using, note the date, the price, and anything the listing said was included or credited. Then note the same items for your house.
If you cannot find those facts, do not treat that sale as a match. Use the ones you can describe.
steps: Pick sold homes that are actually similar.
Write what each sale included or credited.
Drop a sale you cannot describe.

title: Rerun the net after each repair bid
summary: When a written bid arrives, put that number in the calculator before you agree to the work.
body: A bid is a fact. A guess about what the work will cost is not. Type the bid into repair costs and read the new net.
If the net falls below the number you said you would walk away from, skip that project or change the list price on purpose.
Keep the bid with the calculator printout. Later, an offer credit is easier to judge against a number you already accepted.
steps: Enter the bid as a repair cost.
Compare the new net with your walk-away number.
Save the bid and the printout together.

title: Keep price notes in writing
summary: After each pricing talk, write the price, the net, and what you decided.
body: A phone call is easy to remember wrong. When you finish a talk about price, write three lines: the price discussed, the net you calculated, and what you agreed to do next.
Store those notes with your offer page. If a later conversation drifts, you can read what you already decided.
This is your record. It is not a promise to a buyer until you sign something that says so.
steps: Write the price and the net after each talk.
Add the next step you agreed to.
File the note with your offer papers.

title: Shoot in the order a visitor walks
summary: Start at the street, then move through the house in the order someone would walk it.
body: Take the front of the house first, from the sidewalk if you can do that without standing in the road. Then the entry, then each main room in walking order.
That order helps you notice a closet door left open or a light still off. It also gives you a set that tells a simple story.
Save the detail shots for the end: a finished repair, a fireplace, a view from a window. Lead with the rooms.
steps: Photograph the front before you go inside.
Move room to room in walking order.
Add detail shots after the wide shots.

title: Move cars before the photo appointment
summary: Clear the driveway and the curb in front of the house so the photo shows the property.
body: A car in the driveway hides the garage and the walk. Move vehicles off the driveway before the photographer arrives, or before you take the shots yourself.
Ask a neighbor only if you need a place to park for an hour. Do not block their drive.
Check the curb for bins. Roll them out of the frame, then bring them back when you are done.
steps: Move vehicles off the driveway.
Roll bins out of the frame.
Look once from the sidewalk before you shoot.

title: Close lids and hide trash cans
summary: Shut toilet lids, tuck trash cans into cabinets, and clear the edge of every tub.
body: Bath photos pick up small clutter first. Close the lid, put the trash can inside a cabinet, and move bottles off the tub edge.
Hang towels straight or remove them. A heap of used towels is not a styling choice.
Do the same in a kitchen: close the dishwasher and put the sponge out of the frame.
steps: Close toilet lids.
Put trash cans in a cabinet.
Clear bottles off the tub and sponges off the sink.

title: Take one wide shot and one detail
summary: For each main room, keep one photo that shows the whole room and one that shows a finished feature.
body: Stand in a corner and fit the room in one frame with the camera level. That is the wide shot.
Then move closer to one thing you finished: a repaired window, a clear counter, a made bed. That is the detail.
Delete extra frames that repeat the same angle. A short set is easier to sort than a full roll of near-duplicates.
steps: Take one level wide shot of each main room.
Take one closer shot of something you finished.
Delete frames that repeat the same angle.

title: Delete blurry frames the same day
summary: Review the set before you upload it, and drop any frame that is dark, tilted, or soft.
body: Look at each photo on a larger screen than the camera. A frame that looks fine on a phone can be soft on a listing page.
Delete shots with a tilted line, a dark corner you did not mean, or a reflection of the photographer. Retake the room if you have no clean wide shot.
Name the keepers by room so you can find them later. Do this the same day, while you can still reopen a shade and try again.
steps: Review every frame on a large screen.
Delete soft, dark, or tilted shots.
Retake a room if the wide shot is not clean.

title: Price the hours you will spend
summary: Write the tasks you would take on, then estimate the hours before you decide to sell it yourself.
body: List showings, calls, form review, and offer replies as separate lines. Next to each line, write the hours you can actually give it in a normal week.
If the hours are more than you have, that task is a reason to hire help or to pay someone for that piece only.
This is a schedule, not a judgment. The commission calculator can show the money. The hour list shows the time.
steps: List each task you would keep.
Write the hours you can give it.
Hire out a task that does not fit the week.

title: Decide who answers buyer questions
summary: Name the person who will reply, and decide that replies go in writing.
body: Buyers ask about inclusions, repairs, and timing. Pick one person to answer so two people do not give two versions.
Reply in writing, even when the question arrived by phone. A short note is enough: what you were asked, and what you said.
If you hire an agent, ask how those questions will be logged. If you do not, the log is yours.
steps: Name one person to answer.
Put each reply in writing.
Keep the notes with the offer file.

title: Learn which forms you must use
summary: Before you advertise, ask which seller forms your state expects and where to get them.
body: Rules vary by state. A form that worked for a friend in another state may not be the one you need.
Ask a local real-estate attorney or the office that handles closings which seller disclosures you must complete. Write the list down.
Do this before the listing goes live. Filling out a form after a buyer asks is slower, and it is easier to miss a page.
steps: Ask which seller forms your state expects.
Write the list and where to get each form.
Complete them before you start showings.

title: Plan showing hours before you advertise
summary: Choose the days and hours you can leave the house, and write them down before the first call.
body: Showings need an empty-enough house and someone to lock up. Pick hours you can keep for the next few weeks.
Decide how a visitor gets in: you meet them, an agent uses a lockbox, or you hire a sitter for the door. Write that choice next to the hours.
If you cannot offer those hours, that is a reason to hire help rather than a reason to guess.
steps: Write the days and hours you can offer.
Decide how a visitor gets in.
Share that plan before the first request.

title: Write what you will not negotiate
summary: Before the first call, list the terms you will discuss and the ones you will not.
body: Price is not the only term. Closing date, credits, and what stays with the house all move. Write which of those you will talk about.
Write one or two items you will not trade, such as a move-out date you already booked. Read that list before you answer a caller.
You can change the list later. You should not invent it while you are on the phone.
steps: List the terms you will discuss.
List the terms you will not trade.
Read the list before you answer a call.

title: Answer an offer in writing
summary: Send a written yes, no, or counter, even when you already talked it through.
body: A spoken answer is easy to remember two different ways. After you decide, write the decision in a sentence and send it the way your forms require.
Include the price, the credits, and the dates you are accepting or changing. Leave out anything you have not decided.
Save a copy in the offer file the same day. If a second offer arrives, you will want the first answer on paper.
steps: Write the decision in a sentence.
Include price, credits, and dates.
Save a copy in the offer file.

title: Split price from the closing date
summary: When you counter, change the price on one line and the closing date on another.
body: A counter that changes price and date in one breath is hard to compare. Write the price you want on its own line.
Write the closing date you can actually meet on the next line. If you need a few more days to move, say that as a date, not as a feeling.
Then read both lines against your net page. A higher price with a date you cannot keep is not a better offer.
steps: Put the price on one line.
Put the closing date on the next line.
Check both against the net you already wrote.

title: List what stays before you sign
summary: Write the appliances, fixtures, and window coverings that stay, and the items you will take.
body: Offers often assume the appliances stay. If you plan to take a refrigerator, a curtain rod, or a mirror, write that down before you sign.
Walk the house with the list. Point at each item and mark stay or goes. Do this in daylight so you do not forget a shelf in the garage.
Attach the list to your counter or your acceptance. A list you only remember is not part of the deal.
steps: Walk the house and mark stay or goes.
Include the garage and the shed.
Attach the list to the paper you sign.

title: Ask who pays for requested repairs
summary: When a buyer asks for a repair, write the cost and who pays it before you agree.
body: A request to fix something is a money question. Get a bid or write a credit amount before you say yes.
Note who orders the work and who pays. A credit you give at closing is different from a repair you finish before the final walk.
Put the choice in the written response. Then rerun your net with that amount filled in.
steps: Get a bid or name a credit.
Write who orders the work and who pays.
Rerun your net with that amount.

title: Save every counter you send
summary: Keep a copy of each counter in one folder, in the order you sent them.
body: Counters pile up. Number them by date and keep the signed or sent copy, not only the draft.
When a new version arrives, read it next to the one you sent. Highlight only the lines that changed.
If you have an agent, ask for the same set in your folder. If you do not, you are the one who files it.
steps: Save each counter the day you send it.
Number them by date.
Compare each new paper with the one before it.

title: Read the settlement statement when it arrives
summary: Check the price, credits, and payoff on the statement the day you receive it.
body: The statement is the math of the sale. Read the sale price, the payoff, the credits you agreed to, and the amount you are supposed to receive.
Compare those lines with your net page and the signed offer. Circle anything that does not match.
Call the closing office about a mismatch before the appointment, not in the lobby. Bring the circled page with you.
steps: Read price, payoff, credits, and your proceeds.
Circle lines that do not match the contract.
Ask about those lines before closing day.

title: Match the move-out date to the contract
summary: Read the date you must be out, and book the move to finish before that day.
body: The contract date and the date you hoped for can differ. Find the possession line and write it on your calendar.
Book the truck so the house is empty before that day, with a spare hour for keys and a last look.
If you need to stay longer, that is a written change, not a favor you mention at the table.
steps: Find the possession date in the contract.
Put it on your calendar.
Book the move to finish before that day.

title: Gather keys and openers in one envelope
summary: Put every key, garage opener, and gate code in one labeled envelope before closing day.
body: Search the hooks, the car, and the junk drawer. Buyers expect the keys that operate the house you sold.
Label the envelope with the property address. Write gate or alarm codes on a card inside, and keep a copy for yourself until the sale is recorded.
Do not pack the envelope in a moving box. Carry it to closing.
steps: Collect keys, openers, and codes.
Label one envelope with the address.
Carry it to closing instead of packing it.

title: Check your name against your ID
summary: Read the name on the deed papers and make sure it matches the identification you will bring.
body: A missing middle initial or a former name can stall a signing. Compare the papers with the identification you plan to bring.
If the names differ, tell the closing office as soon as you notice. Bring the document that connects the two names if you have one.
Put that identification with the envelope of keys so it is not still in a drawer on closing morning.
steps: Read the name on the deed papers.
Compare it with the identification you will bring.
Tell the closing office if the names differ.

title: Leave utility numbers for the final reading
summary: Write the account numbers and schedule the final readings for the possession date.
body: Call each utility and ask for a final reading on the day you give up possession. Write the confirmation number.
Keep the account numbers on one card in your closing folder. You will want them if a bill arrives after you leave.
Do not shut a service off early if the contract says the house stays heated or lit until possession. Match the shutoff to the date you already signed.
steps: Schedule a final reading for the possession date.
Write the account and confirmation numbers.
Match any shutoff to the date in the contract.

title: Measure doors before you book a truck
summary: Measure the sofa, the mattress, and the narrowest doorway before you reserve a truck.
body: A piece that fit on the way in may not fit if you have added a railing or if the truck plan skips a turn.
Write the height and width of the largest pieces and of the smallest doorway they must pass. Share those numbers with the mover or use them yourself.
If a piece will not pass, decide now whether it stays, gets sold, or needs a different door. Do not decide that on the truck ramp.
steps: Measure the largest furniture and the narrowest door.
Write the numbers down.
Decide the plan for anything that will not pass.

title: Pack a first-week kitchen box
summary: Fill one box with the pan, mugs, soap, and towels you will want before the rest is unpacked.
body: Choose one sturdy box and mark it OPEN FIRST on two sides. Put in a pan, a knife, mugs, soap, towels, and any medicine you take daily.
Load that box in your own car, not in the back of the truck. If the truck is late, you can still cook and wash.
Tape a short list to the top so you do not reopen it to check what you packed.
steps: Pack one box with the first week's kitchen basics.
Mark it OPEN FIRST on two sides.
Carry it in your car.

title: Forward the mail before you leave
summary: File the mail forward in time for it to start on your possession date.
body: Submit the forward with the post office before moving week, and write the start date to match the day you give up the house.
Tell the closing office, your insurer, and anyone you pay on a bill. A forward does not update those accounts by itself.
Keep the confirmation with your closing folder. Check it once after you arrive.
steps: File the mail forward before moving week.
Update accounts that will not follow the forward.
Save the confirmation with your closing papers.

title: Photograph the empty rooms on the last day
summary: Take a photo of each empty room, plus the meter readings, before you lock the door.
body: After the furniture is out, walk the house once. Photograph each room, the inside of the refrigerator, and any scratch you want to remember.
Photograph the meter readings the same hour if you can. Those frames answer questions later without a debate about memory.
Store the photos with your settlement papers, not only on a camera roll you might clear.
steps: Photograph each empty room.
Photograph meter readings.
Save the set with your settlement papers.

title: Carry the closing papers with you
summary: Keep the signed settlement set in your car, not in a box on the truck.
body: Put the signed papers, the key envelope copy, and your identification in one folder. That folder rides with you.
If you need a page while the truck is in transit, you still have it. A box labeled OFFICE is not the same as a folder in the front seat.
When you arrive, file the folder before you unpack the kitchen. You will not want to hunt for it later.
steps: Put signed papers in one folder.
Carry the folder in your car.
File it before you unpack.
